HURRICANE HELENE LEFT A SWATH OF DESTRUCTION ACROSS THE SOUTHEAST, IMPACTING AN AREA STRETCHING FROM THE GULF COAST TO THE SOUTHERN APPALACHIANS. TIMBER DAMAGE ESTIMATES RANGE FROM HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS TO OVER $1 BILLION IN THE AFFECTED STATES. IN THE WAKE OF HELENE FEDERAL, STATE, INDUSTRY AND PRIVATE LAND MANAGERS ARE FACED WITH MANY CHALLENGES. THESE INCLUDE COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH INSECT PESTS AND FOREST PATHOGENS FOLLOWING DISTURBANCE, THE NATURE AND SEVERITY OF DAMAGE AS IT RELATES TO FOREST STRUCTURE AND COMPOSITION, TREE-LEVEL DECLINE AND MORTALITY OVER TIME DUE TO SUBLETHAL DAMAGE, AND RISK OF INVASIVE PLANT SPREAD DUE TO HABITAT CHANGES AND MANAGEMENT INTERVENTIONS. INVASION BY NON-NATIVE PLANTS CAUSES A WIDE ARRAY OF DETRIMENTAL IMPACTS TO U.S. FOREST ECOSYSTEMS, INCLUDING THE DEGRADATION OF WILDLIFE HABITAT, CHANGES TO ECOSYSTEM FUNCTIONS, AND ALTERATIONS TO NUTRIENT, CARBON AND WATER CYCLES. THIS AGREEMENT WILL ALLOW FOR CONDUCTING ASSESSMENTS OF THE RISK OF INVASIVE PLANT ESTABLISHMENT AND SPREAD WITHIN HELENE-AFFECTED FORESTS USING A VARIETY OF FIELD-COLLECTED AND REMOTELY SENSED DATA; PROVIDING DECISION SUPPORT FOR THE MANAGEMENT AND RESTORATION OF THESE FORESTS RELATING TO THE CONTROL OF INVASIVE PLANT ESTABLISHMENT AND SPREAD; AND COMMUNICATING WITH PARTNERS WITHIN THE FOREST SERVICE AND IN OTHER AGENCIES TO SHARE RESULTS.

TO ANALYZE DATA ON WILDLAND FUELS IN AREAS AFFECTED BY HURRICANE HELENE (SOUTHERN APPALACHIAN FORESTED REGION), RUN COMPUTER MODELS OF FIRE BEHAVIOR, AND WORK WITH MANAGERS TO UNDERSTAND HURRICANE DAMAGE AND EFFECTS ON FUTURE FIRE MANAGEMENT AND IMPROVE FUELS MONITORING EFFORTS. DAMAGE CAUSED BY HURRICANE HELENE IS PROFOUND AND WE NOW CAN DO AN ACCURATE ASSESSMENT OF THE HURRICANE DAMAGE, INCLUDING CHANGE IN HAZARDOUS FUELS CONDITIONS USING NEW TECHNOLOGIES (TERRESTRIAL LASER SCANNING), FIELD SAMPLING, AND EMERGING FIRE BEHAVIOR MODELS AND ANALYZE THEM USING SOPHISTICATED COMPUTER PROGRAMS. THIS WILL BUILD PATHWAYS TO LINK THESE UNIQUE (DAMAGED FOREST) FUELS DATA TO FIRE BEHAVIOR MODELS AND PROVIDE ESTIMATES OF FIRE BEHAVIOR IN THESE DAMAGED AREAS. THIS PROJECT WILL EXAMINE FLOODPLAIN PROCESSES AND SITE-SPECIFIC CONDITIONS IN MUNICIPAL WATERSHEDS OF OREGON AND WASHINGTON TO DETERMINE LOCATIONS FOR STRATEGIC RECONNECTION WORK DESIGNED TO REDUCE POST-WILDFIRE FINE SEDIMENT LOADS. THE WORK WILL PRODUCE A COMPREHENSIVE SET OF PRODUCTS THAT IDENTIFY REACH-SCALE FLOODPLAIN RESTORATION POTENTIAL RELATED TO WATER QUALITY RESILIENCE TO WILDFIRE. RESULTS WILL BE SHARED THROUGH PUBLICATIONS AND PRESENTATIONS TO SUPPORT FOREST MANAGERS, WILDFIRE PLANNING, RESTORATION PRACTITIONERS, LOCAL COMMUNITY WATER SUPPLY MANAGERS, AND LANDSCAPE-SCALE PLANNERS. IF THIS AWARD IS NOT APPROVED, THE FOREST SERVICE AND PARTNERS WILL HAVE LITTLE GUIDANCE IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF REGIONALLY AND LOCALLY INFORMED FLOODPLAIN RESTORATION PROJECTS THAT ARE DESIGNED WITH THE GOAL OF REDUCING WATER QUALITY IMPAIRMENT FOLLOWING WILDFIRE. WITHOUT THIS WORK, FOREST MANAGERS AND MUNICIPAL WATER SUPPLIERS WILL LACK PRACTICAL, SCIENCE-BASED GUIDANCE TO SITE FLOODPLAIN RECONNECTION PROJECTS, REDUCING EFFICACY OF UPSLOPE WILDFIRE SEVERITY TREATMENTS AND MAKING WATERSHEDS LESS RESILIENT TO WILDFIRE. THIS HAS THE POTENTIAL TO AFFECT LONG-TERM FOREST PRODUCTIVITY AND HUMAN COMMUNITY RECOVERY TO WILDFIRE.

THIS PROJECT SUPPORTS RESEARCH ON THE EFFECTS OF THINNING AND PRESCRIBED BURNING TREATMENTS ON IMPROVING FOREST HEALTH AND INCREASING RESILIENCE TO WILDFIRE. WORK WILL OCCUR AT EXISTING AND NEWLY ESTABLISHED STUDY SITES IN HIGH-ELEVATION AND LOWER-ELEVATION DRY CONIFER FORESTS THAT HAVE EXPERIENCED HARVEST, PRESCRIBED FIRE, OR WILDFIRE. FIELD ACTIVITIES INCLUDE COLLECTING DATA ON TREE CHARACTERISTICS, TREE SURVIVAL, FIRE-CAUSED INJURY, BARK BEETLE ATTACK, BLISTER RUST PREVALENCE, AND FUEL LOADING TO EVALUATE HOW TREATMENTS AND WILDFIRE AFFECT FOREST STRUCTURE, COMPOSITION, AND LONG-TERM ECOSYSTEM RESPONSES. THE EFFORT INCLUDES DEVELOPING PUBLICATIONS AND TECHNOLOGY-TRANSFER MATERIALS TO INFORM LAND MANAGERS ON NATIONAL FORESTS, PRIVATE LAND MANAGERS AND FORESTRY RESEARCHERS. THIS RESEARCH DIRECTLY SUPPORTS PRIORITIES OF THE FOREST SERVICE (FS), INCLUDING ACTIVE MANAGEMENT FOR FOREST HEALTH AND PRODUCTIVITY, STRENGTHENED PARTNERSHIPS THAT PRODUCE ON-THE-GROUND OUTCOMES, AND PROTECTION OF COMMUNITIES AND NATURAL RESOURCES FROM WILDFIRE. THE PROJECT WILL BE ACCOMPLISHED THROUGH COORDINATED FIELD DATA COLLECTION, ANALYSIS, AND SYNTHESIS. RESPONSIBILITIES INCLUDE DOCUMENTING TREATMENT AND WILDFIRE EFFECTS; COLLECTING, STORING, AND MANAGING DATA AND PRODUCING MANUSCRIPTS AND GUIDANCE DOCUMENTS IN COLLABORATION WITH THE FS. THE FS WILL PROVIDE PROTOCOLS, SAMPLING EQUIPMENT, COMPUTERS, SAFETY AND TECHNICAL TRAINING, AND GUIDANCE ON INFORMATION SYNTHESIS AND PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT. RESULTS WILL BE SHARED AT SCIENTIFIC CONFERENCES SUCH AS THE INTERNATIONAL FIRE ECOLOGY AND MANAGEMENT CONGRESS AND THE WHITEBARK PINE SCIENCE AND MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE. THE WORK CONTRIBUTES TO LONG-TERM RESEARCH, SUPPORTS DEVELOPMENT OF PEER-REVIEWED PUBLICATIONS, AND PROVIDES MANAGERSSUCH AS SILVICULTURISTS, FUELS SPECIALISTS, AND PLANNING STAFFWITH INFORMATION NEEDED TO DESIGN, IMPLEMENT, AND EVALUATE THINNING AND BURNING TREATMENTS CONSISTENT WITH FS PRIORITIES.
